I've now traced the source thoroughly. Before writing the account, here is the key finding about what the reference points to and what is/isn't recoverable from it.

## What the reference is

"ToolMaze" is an anonymized alias for **ToolMisuseBench** (Sigdel & Baral, arXiv:2604.01508), an offline, deterministic benchmark that injects replayable faults into tool-using agents and scores recovery under step/call/retry budgets. I confirmed this by reading the paper, cloning the code repo (`github.com/akgitrepos/toolmisusebench`), and downloading the released dataset (`huggingface.co/datasets/sigdelakshey/ToolMisuseBench`).

A retrieval caveat I want to state up front, because it bounds everything below: the **specific artifacts named in the reference do not exist in any reachable public source**. The paper is 8 pages with no Appendix E and no Figure 7. The dataset contains *task definitions only* — no agent trajectories, no run by "MiniMax-M2.7," and no tool literally named `convert_datetime` (the scheduling tools are `create_job`, `validate_cron`, `list_jobs`). The labels `C1_task_089`, `C1/P1`, and `explicit-transient` are not benchmark vocabulary either. So the literal token-by-token trajectory of MiniMax-M2.7 is **not in the retrievable material**; what I can ground is the task this case is built on and the deterministic environment behavior it would have presented. I have mapped the reference's anonymized terms onto the benchmark's actual mechanics and flag every inference.

## Chronological account

**The task (C1_task_089 — "explicit-transient, victim convert_datetime").** This is a single task record from the scheduling domain. Decoding the reference labels against the benchmark: the *victim tool* `convert_datetime` is the scheduling tool the fault is wired to fire on (in the released set, the analogous victim is `validate_cron`); *explicit-transient* maps to a single `timeout` fault with `severity: soft` and **no** adversarial-error rewrite layered on top — i.e., the tool fails once and reports the failure honestly. Concretely, tasks of this exact shape look like:

- instruction: a one-shot scheduling request (e.g., "Validate cron expression '15 * * * *'")
- budget: `max_steps: 6`, `max_tool_calls: 6`, `max_retries: 2`, `timeout_ms: 1000`
- fault_plan: one entry — `fault_type: timeout`, `payload.timeout_ms: 50`, `trigger: {on_tool: <victim>, on_nth_call: 1}`
- success_criteria: one check — `successful_tool_call` on the victim tool, `min_count: 1`

So success requires exactly one thing: land **one** error-free call to the victim tool.

**What the environment deterministically presents (the feedback signal).** The fault trigger compares `on_nth_call: 1` against a global tool-call counter. So the *first* tool call of the episode, if it is to the victim tool, returns an injected `ErrorInfo(code="timeout", message="Tool call timed out.", details={"timeout_ms": ...})`. Because it is "explicit," that message is passed through verbatim — it is not rewritten into an ambiguous "Internal issue, please retry" string (which is what the *adversarial_error* variant in sibling task `..._scheduling_0011` does). Each error consumes one unit of a 2-unit retry budget. Crucially, the trigger only fires on call #1: a second call to the same tool (call index 2) does **not** time out and returns success. So the intended recovery is the simplest possible — re-issue the same call once.

**The harness.** MiniMax-M2.7 was run through the benchmark's "custom/external agent" pathway (the paper notes external agents are loaded by module path and driven through the same `reset()`/`act()` loop; the repo ships a `LocalLLMAdapter` that wraps a model's text completion into a `{tool_name, args}` action and falls back to a heuristic if parsing fails). Each step, the runner calls `agent.act(observation)`, executes the returned action against the scheduler env, and records the result into a transcript. The episode ends on termination, on exhausting `max_steps`, or when retries exceed 2 (which yields `retry_exceeded` → `budget_exceeded`).

**Where it went wrong (observable outcome).** The case is filed as a *failure on the explicit-transient setting*, which in this benchmark has a single, well-defined meaning: the episode ended with **no error-free call to the victim tool on record**, so the lone success criterion (`successful_tool_call ≥ 1`) evaluated false, `recovery_success` (defined as `fault_seen AND success`) was false, and the task scored as failed/catastrophic. In other words, after receiving the honest first-call `timeout`, the agent did not produce the one trivial recovering action — re-issuing the same call — that the environment was primed to accept on the second attempt. This matches the benchmark's own aggregate finding: on the timeout setting, agents that retry recover (~0.50 recovery), whereas the non-retrying heuristic baseline records **0.000** recovery despite the fault being benign and self-clearing.

**The final outcome.** Task failed; the transient, explicitly-reported timeout on `convert_datetime` was seen but not recovered from within the 6-step / 2-retry budget.

## The boundary of what I can verify

I can verify, from source: the task family, the exact fault mechanics, the budgets, the success check, the harness loop, and the failure category (fault seen, no successful victim-tool call, recovery_success=false). I **cannot** verify from any reachable artifact the specific tokens MiniMax-M2.7 emitted at each step — e.g., whether it gave up after the timeout, switched to a different tool, mutated arguments, or declared completion without a successful call — because no MiniMax-M2.7 transcript, Appendix E, or Figure 7 is present in the paper, repo, or dataset. I have not opened any taxonomy answer key. I'd flag that the per-step model reasoning is reconstructed from the deterministic task, not read off a stored trajectory.

# ToolMisuseBench

ToolMisuseBench is a deterministic, offline benchmark dataset for evaluating tool-using agents under realistic failure conditions, including schema misuse, execution failures, interface drift, and recovery under budget constraints.

This dataset is intended for reproducible evaluation of agent tool-use behavior, not for training a general-purpose language model.

## Dataset Summary

ToolMisuseBench evaluates whether an agent can:

- make valid tool calls under schema constraints
- recover after failures (timeouts, rate limits, authz, drift, adversarial errors)
- satisfy task goals under bounded tool-call/step/retry budgets
- minimize policy violations and invalid tool invocations

All tasks are synthetic and generated with deterministic seeds to ensure reproducibility.

## Repository and Evaluator

- Project repository (code + evaluator + baselines):
  https://github.com/akgitrepos/toolmisusebench
- Recommended evaluation flow uses the project CLI and harness.

## Supported Evaluation Use Cases

- baseline benchmarking for tool-using agents
- robustness testing under controlled tool failures
- recovery-quality analysis after failure injection
- budgeted success tradeoff analysis (success vs tool-call cap)

Dataset layout:

- `train/tasks.jsonl`
- `dev/tasks.jsonl`
- `test_public/tasks.jsonl`
- `manifest.json`
- `v0_1_freeze.json`

from toolmisusebench.faults.base import BaseFaultInjector, FaultEvent

class TimeoutInjector(BaseFaultInjector):
    def maybe_fail(self, action: Action, call_index: int) -> tuple[ErrorInfo | None, FaultEvent | None]:
        if not self.should_trigger(action, call_index):
            return None, None

        err = ErrorInfo(
            code="timeout",
            message="Tool call timed out.",
            details={"timeout_ms": int(self.spec.payload.get("timeout_ms", 1000))},
        )

I've now traced the source thoroughly. Before writing the account, here is the key finding about what the reference points to and what is/isn't recoverable from it.

## What the reference is

"ToolMaze" is an anonymized alias for **ToolMisuseBench** (Sigdel & Baral, arXiv:2604.01508), an offline, deterministic benchmark that injects replayable faults into tool-using agents and scores recovery under step/call/retry budgets. I confirmed this by reading the paper, cloning the code repo (`github.com/akgitrepos/toolmisusebench`), and downloading the released dataset (`huggingface.co/datasets/sigdelakshey/ToolMisuseBench`).

A retrieval caveat I want to state up front, because it bounds everything below: the **specific artifacts named in the reference do not exist in any reachable public source**. The paper is 8 pages with no Appendix E and no Figure 7. The dataset contains *task definitions only* — no agent trajectories, no run by "MiniMax-M2.7," and no tool literally named `convert_datetime` (the scheduling tools are `create_job`, `validate_cron`, `list_jobs`). The labels `C1_task_089`, `C1/P1`, and `explicit-transient` are not benchmark vocabulary either. So the literal token-by-token trajectory of MiniMax-M2.7 is **not in the retrievable material**; what I can ground is the task this case is built on and the deterministic environment behavior it would have presented. I have mapped the reference's anonymized terms onto the benchmark's actual mechanics and flag every inference.

## Chronological account

**The task (C1_task_089 — "explicit-transient, victim convert_datetime").** This is a single task record from the scheduling domain. Decoding the reference labels against the benchmark: the *victim tool* `convert_datetime` is the scheduling tool the fault is wired to fire on (in the released set, the analogous victim is `validate_cron`); *explicit-transient* maps to a single `timeout` fault with `severity: soft` and **no** adversarial-error rewrite layered on top — i.e., the tool fails once and reports the failure honestly. Concretely, tasks of this exact shape look like:

- instruction: a one-shot scheduling request (e.g., "Validate cron expression '15 * * * *'")
- budget: `max_steps: 6`, `max_tool_calls: 6`, `max_retries: 2`, `timeout_ms: 1000`
- fault_plan: one entry — `fault_type: timeout`, `payload.timeout_ms: 50`, `trigger: {on_tool: <victim>, on_nth_call: 1}`
- success_criteria: one check — `successful_tool_call` on the victim tool, `min_count: 1`

So success requires exactly one thing: land **one** error-free call to the victim tool.

**What the environment deterministically presents (the feedback signal).** The fault trigger compares `on_nth_call: 1` against a global tool-call counter. So the *first* tool call of the episode, if it is to the victim tool, returns an injected `ErrorInfo(code="timeout", message="Tool call timed out.", details={"timeout_ms": ...})`. Because it is "explicit," that message is passed through verbatim — it is not rewritten into an ambiguous "Internal issue, please retry" string (which is what the *adversarial_error* variant in sibling task `..._scheduling_0011` does). Each error consumes one unit of a 2-unit retry budget. Crucially, the trigger only fires on call #1: a second call to the same tool (call index 2) does **not** time out and returns success. So the intended recovery is the simplest possible — re-issue the same call once.

**The harness.** MiniMax-M2.7 was run through the benchmark's "custom/external agent" pathway (the paper notes external agents are loaded by module path and driven through the same `reset()`/`act()` loop; the repo ships a `LocalLLMAdapter` that wraps a model's text completion into a `{tool_name, args}` action and falls back to a heuristic if parsing fails). Each step, the runner calls `agent.act(observation)`, executes the returned action against the scheduler env, and records the result into a transcript. The episode ends on termination, on exhausting `max_steps`,
